title: Strong earthquake with preliminary magnitude of 5.7 strikes Japan

 Strong earthquake with preliminary magnitude of 5.7 strikes Japan
 Listen Listen Text Size Print Summary
 Close summary A magnitude-5.7 earthquake struck central Japan at 1:04 a.m. Sunday, injuring at least 22 people and damaging store windows. The Japan Meteorological Agency placed the quake in Shizuoka Prefecture, about 40 kilometers below the surface, while the U.S. Geological Survey reported a magnitude of 5.5. The strongest shaking was felt in Aichi, and Shinkansen trains slowed as a precaution.
 Key Facts
 The affected area included Hamamatsu, Kyoto, Nara, Yamanashi and Gifu.
 Some people were injured after falling on stairs while trying to flee.
 Smaller aftershocks were reported following the quake.
 By AP Published Nov 8, 2026 8:35 am KST
 Updated Nov 8, 2026 9:32 am KST
 An aerial view shows the damaged Aeon Mall shopping centre after an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.1 struck Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture in Kashima Town, Kumamoto Prefecture, Japan, July 28. Kyodo via Reuters-Yonhap
 TOKYO — A strong earthquake shook central Japan early Sunday, shattering store windows, causing people to flee buildings and leaving at least 22 people injured, according to local media.
 Japan’s Meteorological Agency put the quake’s magnitude at 5.7, while the U.S. Geological Survey reported it at magnitude 5.5. Smaller aftershocks were reported.
 A wide area near Aichi Prefecture was affected, including the city of Hamamatsu, the ancient capitals of Kyoto and Nara and nearby prefectures of Yamanashi, where Mount Fuji is located, as well as Gifu.
 Japanese TV footage showed shattered store windows and scattered shards of glass on the streets. A bookstore was left with mounds of books that had flown off the shelves. The injuries included people who fell from stairs while they were trying to flee.
 The quake, which struck at 1:04 a.m., was located about 40 kilometers (25 miles) below the earth's surface in Shizuoka Prefecture. Aichi and Shizuoka are neighboring regions. They are far enough from Tokyo that the quake was not felt there. The most violent shaking was felt in Aichi, according to official seismic assessments.
 The Shinkansen bullet trains were running at slower speeds in the affected areas as a precautionary measure. Sometimes quakes can damage the railways the trains run on.
 Japan is located in an area that is prone to earthquakes.
